body.text: As parliament returns without Helen Haines, federal MPs are encouraged to sign a civility pledge that the independent MP backed.

Scarr calls for MPs and senators to consider conduct
Liberal senator Paul Scarr says there's been a "serious deterioration" in rhetoric over the past 18 months.
"I think all of us need to consider how we conduct ourselves," he tells reporters on his way into Parliament House this morning.

"I've noticed over the last 18 months, there's been a serious deterioration in terms of the … passions that are unleashed in terms of political debate and the vitriol and the abuse, especially online abuse."
Scarr's remarks come after AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett told ABC's Insiders there was a correlation between some political discourse and threats to parliamentarians.
Farley says he hasn't seen One Nation's cartoons
One Nation MP David Farley says he hasn't watched his party's Please Explain cartoons, which include storylines of politicians being run over.

The cartoons have been criticised after AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett told Insiders there was a direct correlation between increasingly heated political debate and threats against MPs and public figures.

Asked about the cartoons, Barrett agreed they were an example of the type of rhetoric that could contribute to escalating abuse and violence. But One Nation leader Pauline Hanson defended the series as "satirical" and said it was "here to stay".
So what does her MP in the House of Reps think?
"I've heard the rhetoric about them being inciting, but I haven't watched a cartoon since I was about 12 years old," Farley says. "I haven't seen them."
"I've heard the rhetoric about them being inciting, but I haven't watched a cartoon since I was about 12 years old," Farley says.
"I haven't seen them."

What is the civility pledge?
Members of the crossbench have backed calls for parliamentarians to sign a civility pledge, inspired by the family of British MP Jo Cox, who was murdered in 2016.
Helen Haines was the first MP to sign the pledge this year.
"In my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect and compassion," it says.
Labor frontbencher Mark Butler tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast he'll have a look over it.
Safety concerns, threats have changed 'dramatically': Butler
Health Minister Mark Butler says this week will be an opportunity for discussion about what more can be done to keep MPs, their families and staff members safe.
The Labor frontbencher says the environment has changed "dramatically" over his 20 years in parliament.
He says federal police have been "very responsive" to requests when there have been threats made against him.
"But the number and the nature of the threats of violence and death, not just to MPs but to their children and to their partners and their staff, is like nothing we saw 20 years ago," he says.
Asked about reports cabinet will consider security upgrades for MPs at a meeting today, Butler says the government is taking security concerns seriously.
"We'll have a very serious, deep discussion about that over the course of this week … and we'll take the advice of the federal police and other security agencies about that."
Security rethink should focus on MPs out in their electorates: Tehan
Security measures across the public areas of Parliament House will be strengthened in response to the attack on Helen Haines last week.
But Liberal frontbencher Dan Tehan says it's the level of protection afforded to MPs in their electorates that is the real issue.

"Whether it's around security for MPs at their homes. I mean, one of the issues … as a rural MP, you're always out in your community in public, like Helen was. And I think that's just probably more an area where we need to be looking at," he tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
"I think the vulnerability is actually when we're out doing our job in the community and that's probably where we need to put the focus."

Joyce raises censorship concerns, Plibersek thinks AFP worth listening to
One Nation's Barnaby Joyce is concerned an attempt to tone down political debate could cross into censorship.
AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett drew a direct link between inflamed political rhetoric and a rise in threats in an interview with ABC's Insiders yesterday.
Speaking with Seven this morning, Joyce said MPs shouldn't have to be warned in the first place.
"I think we shouldn't be in that space to start off with," he says.

"What I always worry about when these things start heading towards censorship. Because censorship is a huge problem for Australia. It's a huge problem for democracy. "You can do two things at the same time ... tone down what you do without bringing about censorship."
"What I always worry about when these things start heading towards censorship. Because censorship is a huge problem for Australia. It's a huge problem for democracy.
"You can do two things at the same time ... tone down what you do without bringing about censorship."
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek, who was also on the panel, thinks the AFP boss should be listened to.

"I think you can have strong and robust debate without being mean or cruel," she says. "If the Australian Federal Police and ASIO are both saying we need to change the way we're having political debates in this country because they are inflaming things and I think we can listen to that."
"I think you can have strong and robust debate without being mean or cruel," she says.

"If the Australian Federal Police and ASIO are both saying we need to change the way we're having political debates in this country because they are inflaming things and I think we can listen to that."
Chaney wants code of conduct to apply to the chamber
A warning from the AFP commissioner about the direct link between political rhetoric and an increase in violent threats is a timely reminder, independent Kate Chaney says.
"Words matter and what we do matters," she tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
Chaney says she'd like for the parliamentary code of conduct to apply also to behaviour in the chamber.
"I think we can still have robust debate and focus on the issue and hold each other to account while also being respectful and civil and surely that's something that we can manage," she says.
Key Event
Crossbench MP to join Haines in signing civility pledge
She was wearing an orange blazer with a cockatoo broach on her lapel as a gesture of support for independent MP Helen Haines.
Federal MPs are being asked to sign a civility pledge. Haines was the first to sign it two months ago.
Chaney says she'll be adding her name to the list.

"This is very much an optional thing. There's no pressure on MPs to do this. I think there's something really symbolic about the fact that Helen was the only federal MP to have signed this, the first," she said.

"It is a very simple thing. It just says: in my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect and compassion. "And that feels to me like a simple and poignant way to honour the contribution Helen's made to the parliament and continue to try to embody those values that she personifies in the way that I do my work in parliament."

Security increased as parliament returns to Canberra without Helen Haines
Parliament returns today with one of its most respected members missing, as MPs reconvene in Canberra without Helen Haines.
Security has been strengthened at Parliament House after a car struck the independent MP outside her Wangaratta electorate office in what police are treating as a deliberate attack.
The 65-year-old mother of three, admired across the political divide for her integrity, has had both legs amputated after suffering severe injuries to her lower body.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is expected to move a motion in the House of Representatives that would set aside much of the day for MPs to offer messages of support.

Haines's seat will be empty at Question Time, with fellow crossbenchers pledging to carry forward her leadership example as parliament grapples with ways to approach security in their respective communities.
